topic: AI creative tools producing soulless, generic, or off-brand work
blind_spots: No first-hand client/executive voices explaining why AI use is mandated despite poor outputs — only practitioner perspectives.
Evidence skews toward anti-AI communities (r/BetterOffline) and creative-protectionist outlets; little counter-evidence from successful AI-assisted workflows.
No discussion of whether fine-tuned, brand-trained, or RAG-augmented models reduce the 'AI look' and off-brand failures.
Failure modes are conflated (technical glitches, brand-tone mismatch, philosophical soullessness, derivative content) — they may have distinct solutions.
No quantitative baseline comparing AI rejection rates to human-only prototype rejection rates.
The 60–80% income-drop statistic from a single source is repeated uncritically without methodology scrutiny.
No engagement with the possibility that some 'AI allegations' stigmatize legitimate human work.
Evidence does not separate text/LLM failures from image, video, and layout tool failures.
contradictions: Practitioners argue failures are architectural ('Large Language models don't understand layout, format, nor style... there's no "AI" application in your space'), while managers/clients insist the fault is insufficient prompt engineering ('spend more time prompt engineering the layout').

Some sources frame soullessness as inherent and unfixable, while MarTech/Mojo frame it as a process problem that can be repaired by adding narrative, control, and lived experience — implying the deficiency is not intrinsic.
Clients simultaneously demand 'innovative' AI workflows and reject the resulting prototypes as toddler-level work.
